Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Baltimore MD/Washington DC
927 PM EDT Mon Sep 7 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
No significant changes were made to this forecast package.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
- 1) Dry through mid week.

- 2) Shower and thunderstorm chances return Thursday.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
KEY MESSAGE 1...Dry through mid week.

The latest surface analysis paints a quiet picture over the area
with sprawling high pressure extending over the Great Lakes into
the Mid-Atlantic states. Conditions remain tranquil this evening
with just some passing mid to high clouds dropping down from 
the upper Mid-Atlantic. The dry nature of the air mass will 
support ample cooling into the night.

High pressure will persist over the Mid-Atlantic through Wednesday
before gradually moving offshore. Large scale subsidence and 
dry air lead to a precipitation-free forecast with temperatures 
rising to several degrees above normal as the high pulls 
offshore. This leads to high temperatures in the mid to upper 
80s Tuesday, perhaps near 90 Wednesday (slightly cooler in the 
mountains). Low temperatures (and dew points) will generally be 
in the 50s and 60s during this time. Some river valley fog is 
likely each morning.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Shower and thunderstorm chances return Thursday.

The upper-level ridge will begin to flatten out Wednesday before 
breaking down and pushing south and east into Thursday. Several 
pieces of upper-level energy rotating around an upper low 
centered over the Hudson Bay will slowly push a cold front south
towards our region by Thursday. At the surface, high pressure 
pushing offshore will bring increasingly warm and humid 
conditions to the area, with highs in the 80s to near 90 with 
dew points in the upper 60s to low 70s, with the highest values 
being Thursday.

Model guidance over the past 24 hours has come into better agreement 
in regards to the progression of the front on Thursday, as well as 
the upper-level pattern in association with it. The front 
really looks like it will flatten out as it moves southward, and
really loses the upper-level support. The timing of peak 
heating and the highest shear just doesn't look to line up at 
this point. There may be some jet-induced showers and storms 
late Thursday as we move into the right entrance of the upper 
jet centered over New England, but not necessarily expecting 
those to be severe at that point, as the front should be largely
through the region. At this point, the severe weather threat 
looks very limited, but any storm that develops on the warm side
of the boundary could bring some gusty winds along with it, but
the lack of a substantial wind field will really make that more
difficult with southward extent.

As this cold front transitions offshore Friday, temps drop again
and conditions become much drier heading into the start of the 
weekend as high pressure moves in overhead. The next system may
approach by late next weekend.

&&

.AVIATION /00Z TUESDAY THROUGH SATURDAY/...
VFR conditions are expected to prevail through the end of the
week, with two exceptions. Early morning river valley fog could
affect mainly KCHO/KMRB each day roughly 08z-13z. Then, some
shower and thunderstorm activity could bring brief restrictions
on Thursday (mainly in the afternoon and/or evening). Light NE
winds today become E to S tonight into Tuesday, then remain S
through Thursday until a cold front brings a shift to W/NW.

&&

.MARINE...
High pressure will result in light northeast winds becoming
south through Tuesday. Winds may increase briefly early
Wednesday morning as the high shifts offshore, but are more
likely to increase in southerly channeling Wednesday afternoon
into Wednesday night. Winds shift to the west and northwest and
could remain gusty Thursday as a cold front crosses, possibly
bringing a few showers and thunderstorms. Winds should become
lighter heading into Friday.

&&

.TIDES/COASTAL FLOODING...
Tide levels remain around 1 to 1.25 feet above normal. With 
light northeast winds becoming southerly, tide levels are likely
to remain relatively steady around 1 foot above astronomical 
norms through the middle of the week. The higher of the two 
diurnal tides is in the later night/early morning period, during
which time Annapolis is most likely to hit minor flood stage 
through early Thursday prior to a cold front shifting winds to 
the west. Other sites like Havre de Grace, Bowley's Quarters, 
and Alexandria could approach minor flood at times, as well.
